newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi court wants proof from heirs in nurses' trial.
newsitem.headline: Saudi court wants proof from heirs in nurses' trial.

text.p: A Saudi court demanded legal proof within a week that the brother of an Australian nurse killed in Saudi Arabia is her heir, which can give him the power to decide about life or death for the accused, the defence lawyers said.

The Islamic sharia court called for the evidence on Sunday when it resumed the trial of British nurses Deborah Parry, 38, and Lucille McLauchlan, 31. They are charged with murdering their 55-year-old colleague Yvonne Gilford in December at a medical complex in the eastern Saudi city of Dhahran.
If they are found guilty of murdering Gilford, they may face the death penalty, which in Saudi Arabia is traditionally public beheading by the sword.

The court also refused to accept the power of attorney from the victim's mother to her son Frank Gilford "until it is established that the power of attorney was given when Mrs M.L. Gilford was mentally competent", the defendents' lawyer Salah al-Hejailan said in a statement.
The victim's 84-year-old mother Muriel suffers from Alzheimer's disease and lives in a nursing home in Australia.

"Preferably the court would like a new power of attorney to be given, together with evidence before the notary public or otherwise that Mrs M.L. Gilford is now mentally competent," the statement sent to Reuters said.

It said the court in the city of Khobar near Dhahran had asked for a private conference with the British and Australian consuls before Sunday's proceedings began. It did not give any details of the meeting.
"The court adjourned the proceedings until Monday, 23 June 1997, in order to allow the Gilford family sufficient time to satisfy the court's requirements," it added.
The court had earlier adjourned on May 15 to give the victim's family three weeks to consider a pre-verdict settlement which could spare the nurses' lives if they were convicted.

Islamic sharia law enforced in Saudi Arabia allows the victim's family to decide for or against execution if the court determines capital punishment is the appropriate sentence. Gilford's brother Frank has said he favours the death penalty.
Alternatively, the victim's family could ask for financial recompense, which is commonly known as "blood money".
Despite letters by the two nurses appealing for the Gilfords' cooperation, the parties did not come to a settlement before Sunday's session, the defence lawyers said.
The court now wanted an official statement from the Gilfords outlining their view on a possible execution before it reaches a verdict, the lawyers' statement said.

"The court wishes to obtain a clear and authoritative statement of the position of the actual heir or heirs as to any death penalty which may be found to apply, before turning then to the public aspect of the case, which...concerns the basic issue of innocence or guilt," the firm said.
